rooms.description: The lean arc42 adaptation every 561 Group game-fleet service specs against: DESIGN.md stays the design-decisions doctrine document (unchanged, unrenamed); a companion ARCHITECTURE.md carries the arc42-numbered engineering record, extended with a house §13 theory binding and §14 ludics section, plus a falsifiable now/next/later roadmap appendix. Written after reading and verifying every existing fleet spec; extends, never replaces, the precedent those specs already set.
rooms.body:
# House Specification Standard

## 0. What this document is, and is not

This is an **engineering document**, not a governance document. It exists because the owner has
explicitly rejected vocabulary empires, process doctrine, and opaque questionnaires — so every
section below either does real work (it changes what an implementing agent writes, or what a
reviewer checks) or it is not here. **A section with nothing true to say about a given service is
omitted from that service's document entirely — never left as a stub, an empty heading, or a
"TBD."** A reader who sees a section present can trust it says something real; a reader who sees
it absent should read that as "nothing here yet," not "someone forgot."

This standard does not invent a new doctrine. Every fleet service already independently converged
on the same shape: pure `.mts` domain modules, one stateful scene, a native HTTP/SSE transport, a
double-entry ledger behind a `PaymentProvider` boundary, deterministic seeded engines, and — since
`onestone-service` — an explicit "the math is load-bearing (and honestly labeled)" section, which
`lantern-service` generalized into "What's load-bearing vs. flavor," which `self-education-platform-design.md`
and `equivo-design.md` extended again with per-row evidence-strength labeling and an explicit
policy for representing absent material as absent rather than synthesized. This standard is the
write-up of that convergence, formalized once so the next service doesn't have to reinvent it, and
extended with two house-specific sections (§13, §14) that name what none of the existing docs name
explicitly: which piece of `@lenticule-science/metrologic` a game's mechanics actually instantiate, and what the
game's core loop is doing as *ludics* — session shape, skill expression, retention — with every
claim tied to evidence rather than asserted.

## 1. Two documents, not one: DESIGN.md stays; ARCHITECTURE.md is new

**RESPECT existing precedent, stated as a hard rule**: this standard does not rename, supplant, or
deprecate any existing `DESIGN.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `README.md`, `DEPLOY.md`, or `TILESLOTS-DESIGN.md`.
`flickering-delve-service/DESIGN.md` originated the house doctrine; `onestone-service/DESIGN.md`
inherits it explicitly ("Doctrine (inherited from flickering-delve-service)"); `lantern-service/DESIGN.md`
added the load-bearing-vs-flavor disclosure section by name. These are **decision documents**: they
answer "what did we decide, and why" in the voice of the team that built the service, and they stay
exactly where they are, exactly as they are.

**`ARCHITECTURE.md` is the new, companion document this standard specifies.** It is an
**engineering record**: it answers "what exists, traced through the actual code, with real numbers"
— module inventories with responsibilities, runtime scenarios traced through real function calls,
ADRs recovered from what the code shows was decided (not re-litigated), a real debt list, a real
theory binding, and a roadmap. Where `DESIGN.md` says "we decided the settle loop terminates by
operator idempotence, not a depth cap," `ARCHITECTURE.md` says "here is the loop
(`engine.mts::settleLoop`), here is the acyclicity argument traced to `FALL_ALIGNMENT_MIN`, here is
the test that exercises it, here is the debt this leaves." The two documents cite each other rather
than duplicate each other — `ARCHITECTURE.md` should assume its reader has `DESIGN.md` open beside
it, and should not restate the design rationale, only ground it.

A service that has no `DESIGN.md` yet writes one *first*, using whatever design-decision doctrine
already exists in the fleet (the section 1 pattern above) — `ARCHITECTURE.md` without a `DESIGN.md`
underneath it is engineering record for decisions no one wrote down, and that gap should be visible,
not backfilled by inventing a `DESIGN.md`'s content inside the wrong document.

## 2. Constraints

Every constraint below is load-bearing on how a service may be built, not aspirational style
guidance. A service that violates one of these is not "done, minus polish" — it has not met the
house bar.

- **The determinism discipline.** No domain module may read `Date.now()` or call `Math.random()`.
  Every function that needs "now" takes it as an injected parameter; every source of randomness is
  a seeded PRNG (the house pattern is FNV-1a hash → mulberry32, independently re-derived in
  `flickering-delve-service/src/seed.mts`, `onestone-service/src/seed.mts`, and `solitaire-service/src/cards.mts`,
  never imported cross-service — see the vendor-not-import rule below). This is not a style
  preference: it is what makes replay verification (§8) possible at all, and what makes "the same
  seed produces the same board for every player" a provable property rather than a hope.
- **The git ban.** No git command may be run in any form, by any agent, on this development
  machine — git causes WSL lockups, and a hook blocks it. Version history, if wanted, is a
  filesystem or corpus-normalization concern, never a reason to shell out to git.
- **The zero-dependency rule.** Domain modules ship on Node builtins only. `@561-group/*` packages
  (via the local Verdaccio registry) are the one licensed exception, and even those are vendored —
  see below — not live-imported across independently-deployed services. `@lenticule-science/metrologic` itself
  holds to zero runtime dependencies across all thirteen of its packages; a game that needs it for
  a checker or a cost function vendors the specific subpath it needs, never the whole catalog live.
- **Vendor a copy, not a cross-service import.** Each service ships its own Dockerfile/deploy unit;
  a live import from one deployed service into another couples two independent deploys for a
  handful of small pure functions. `onestone-service/src/ledger.mts` is a documented near-verbatim
  port of `flickering-delve-service/src/ledger.mts`; `lantern-service/src/stability.mts` is a
  documented vendor of `onestone-service/src/validate.mts`'s pebble-game functions. This standard
  requires that every such port be *documented as a port* at the point of vendoring (a module
  header note naming the source file) — an undocumented duplicate is debt, a documented one is the
  house pattern working correctly.
- **One concern per file, one stateful scene per service.** Pure `.mts` domain modules, each paired
  with a co-located `<name>.test.mts` run under `node --test` (no external test framework). Every
  service isolates its one piece of mutable runtime state behind a single `scene.mts` (or
  equivalent); every other module is a pure function of its arguments. `ARCHITECTURE.md`'s module
  inventory (§5) is where a reviewer checks this constraint actually holds for a given service.
- **Earn-only, no wagering.** No chance-based payout multipliers, no RNG-outcome-scaled rewards, no
  "double or nothing" mechanic, regardless of jurisdiction legality. A board's or a deal's own
  randomness (present for reasons that have nothing to do with money) must never itself scale a
  payout.
- **`node --check`/`-c` has two confirmed traps on this house's own toolchain, both found by
  sabotage-verification (inject a syntax error, confirm the check script actually catches it) —
  a `"check"` script that has never been sabotage-verified should be assumed to have at least the
  first: (1) it only ever syntax-checks its *first* argument, so `node --check src/*.mts` silently
  validates one file and false-greens every other one the shell glob expanded to — the required
  pattern is a per-file loop (`for f in <globs>; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; node --check "$f" ||
  exit 1; done`), never a bare multi-arg invocation; (2) even looped correctly, `node --check` is
  itself a confirmed no-op specifically for `.mts` files in this Node build (v24.19.0) — it exits 0
  on any input, including unparseable garbage, because type-stripping is applied on the *execution*
  path but not on `--check`'s syntax-only path (the identical content as `.mjs` correctly fails).
  `.mts` files therefore need a real gate built from `node:module`'s `stripTypeScriptTypes` plus a
  second pass validating the stripped output as real JS (a temp-file `node --check`, not `new
  Function`, which cannot parse a module's own top-level `import`/`export`) — the reference
  implementation is `check-mts.mjs`, vendored per house doctrine wherever a service's `check`
  script covers `.mts` files (canonical copy: `flickering-delve-service/check-mts.mjs`).

## 3. Context

What sits outside the service and why the service exists relative to it: which fleet-shared
package it depends on (`@lenticule-science/metrologic`, and — once built — `@561-group/cartridge`/`@561-group/energy-bank`
per `cartridge-and-energy-bank-spec.md`), which subdomain it deploys to per the vision note's
`<game-name>.561.group` convention, whether `play.561.group`'s catalog lists it, and who plays it
(human browser players, terminal/API clients, AI players as peers — the vision note's explicit
house stance that these are not three separate integration problems but one manifest-shaped
contract). Omit this section if a service genuinely has no external context worth stating beyond
"it is a game in the fleet" — most services will have real content here (at minimum, the catalog
listing and subdomain).

## 4. Solution strategy

The one or two sentences that explain the whole shape: "the board is a graph, not a grid, so one
match engine serves every tessellation" (onestone); "the world is an append-only fact-trace, so
game state doubles as an auditable ledger with no second state system" (flickering-delve); "every
game converges on seed-in/deterministic-engine/intent-log-out/replay-to-verify, so extract that
shape once as a shared substrate" (the Cartridge/Energy Bank proposal). This section is the
`DESIGN.md`'s "Thesis" restated in one place for a reader who wants the whole architecture in one
paragraph before the module-by-module detail.

## 5. Building block view — the module inventory

A table, not prose: every module, its responsibility in one line, whether it is pure or the
service's one stateful piece, and its real line count and test count (`wc -l`, `node --test`
output — read the file and run the suite, never estimate). This is the section most tempted to go
stale; the rule that keeps it honest is that **every number in this table is one the writer ran or
counted for this document**, not copied from a prior draft or a README that might have drifted.
Group modules by layer where a service has real layers (domain / scene / transport / client) rather
than listing forty files flat.

## 6. Runtime view — real scenarios traced through the code

Not UML sequence diagrams — prose traces of 2-4 real scenarios, each one naming actual function
calls in order, with the file and (where useful) the line range. "A player swaps two adjacent
tiles: `server.mts`'s `/input` route resolves the bearer token, calls `scene.mts`'s `input()`,
which dispatches to `handleSwap`, which calls `engine.mts`'s `applyMove`, which finds matches,
mints specials, resolves blocker hits, falls, refills, and rescans to a fixed point before
`finishOrContinue` checks whether the level just ended." Pick scenarios that exercise the
service's actual hard parts (a cascade, a rekindle, a webhook settle, a guest-to-account
migration) — a scenario that's just "GET / returns HTML" teaches a reader nothing they didn't
already assume.

## 7. Deployment view

How this actually ships: `node src/server.mts` directly (the house's stated no-framework
transport), the deploy target if one is chosen (`onestone-service/DEPLOY.md`'s Cloud Run pattern
is the fleet's first real example — `--max-instances 1` because game state lives in one process,
`--session-affinity` for SSE), environment variables that gate real payment credentials, and the
explicit warning pattern `DEPLOY.md` sets: do not configure real Stripe/Hive/ZBD credentials until
durable state exists and the shared-payment-identity decision is made. A service with no deploy
story yet should say so plainly ("not yet deployed; runs on localhost only") rather than omit the
section — that is itself a debt-list item (§11), not a gap to paper over.

## 8. Crosscutting concepts

The house's non-negotiable cross-cutting properties, each stated as a **checkable claim about this
service**, not a restatement of the general policy:

- **Replay verification.** How this service's anti-cheat actually works: a seed plus an ordered
  intent/move log is replayed server-side through the same pure engine the client ran against, and
  the server never trusts a claimed outcome it cannot re-derive. Name the concrete artifact
  (`solitaire-service`'s move-log, `onestone-service`'s per-move `applyMove` replay, the Cartridge
  spec's `defaultReplay`) and, honestly, whether it exists yet or is roadmap (onestone's own
  `ROADMAP.md`: "no standalone `replay()` exists today," per the cartridge spec's own audit).
- **Ledger invariants.** If the service touches money at all: the chart-of-accounts shape, the
  double-entry balance invariant (`AuditLedger.record` refuses an unbalanced entry outright — an
  invariant of the type, not a runtime check that can be skipped), and — the newer, sharper
  invariant the Energy Bank spec introduces — payouts never exceeding verified revenue, stated as a
  pure function over the ledger's own recomputed balances
  (`verifyPayoutInvariant`), never a cached running counter. A service with no payout path (every
  shipped game today) states that plainly rather than leaving the reader to infer it.
- **Carrier Audit.** For every settlement/economy flow a spec describes — every place a mechanic,
  a purchase, or a payout is presented as "costs nothing," "not consumed," or "free" — state
  explicitly which of three claims that language actually is. Added 2026-08-19 (`wilder-conceptions-01.md`
  item 1, and the same-day ringleader response in that file), after a real overclaim in
  `the-suite-and-the-studio.md` §2 was caught by exactly this discipline and corrected in place —
  read that dated correction as the worked example this bullet exists to generalize, not a
  one-off fix.
  - **Structurally free (a P-invariant).** The claim is backed by a real, checkable balance
    invariant — cite it. `AuditLedger.record`'s refuse-on-unbalanced-entry and the Energy Bank
    spec's `verifyPayoutInvariant` (§ Ledger invariants, above) are the house's working examples:
    a player moving energy between two of their own accounts, or a settle that nets to zero, is
    genuinely free in the sense the ledger can prove, not merely assert.
  - **Priced (a T-invariant).** The claim is true only relative to a projection, and something
    real pays for it *off* that projection — name the actual carrier and where its rate is
    stated. The house's own corrected instance: "we pay you; you are never the product" hid the
    real carrier (ad revenue, shared with the player) behind ledger language that was true on the
    ledger's own coordinates and false about the whole system. The corrected trust copy — "We
    sell ads and share the revenue with the players. We never take your money to play, never let
    you wager it, and never pay out more than we verifiably earned" — is the house's reference
    example of naming the carrier instead of hiding it.
  - **Terminal (a sink).** No invariant makes the spend recoverable — say so plainly, before a
    player commits, not after. A currency that is spent and gone (no P-invariant path back, no
    T-invariant that returns value elsewhere) is not dishonest to offer, but a spec — and, per
    `wilder-conceptions-01.md` item 7's proposed extension of this same discipline into player-
    facing UI, the product itself — that calls a terminal spend "free" or leaves its permanence
    unstated is exactly the failure mode this bullet exists to catch.
  - This is a **documentation discipline against existing invariants, not new code**: every
    settlement flow a service's `ARCHITECTURE.md`/`DESIGN.md` describes should be classifiable as
    one of the three from the code that already exists (a ledger check, a chart-of-accounts
    entry, or the plain absence of either) — a flow this bullet cannot classify from real code is
    itself a finding, not a reason to skip the classification.
- **Ethics as executable tests.** The house's concrete instance is `onestone-service`'s "never a
  level-solvability shortcut" — stated in `types.mts`'s own doc comment on `Sku['grant']`, and
  enforced by `validate.mts`'s pebble-game oracle actually gating which levels ship. Name this
  service's own ethical constraint, if it has one distinct from the general no-wagering/earn-only
  rules in §2, and name the test (not the policy prose) that would fail if the constraint were
  violated.
- **Accessibility.** Keyboard-completeness, screen-reader announcements for state changes, no
  color-only signals, `prefers-reduced-motion` respected. `solitaire-service/DESIGN.md`'s keyboard
  coverage test ("a static test enumerates every move kind `engine` exposes and asserts `client`'s
  keymap table binds a key to it — a new move kind with no keyboard binding fails CI, not a manual
  accessibility audit") is the house pattern to match: accessibility as a CI-checked property of
  the code, not a review checklist item that can silently rot.

## 9. Decisions (ADRs)

Architecture decisions **recovered from what the code shows was decided**, not invented for this
document. Each ADR: the decision, the alternative(s) it closes off, and the evidence in the code
that the decision was actually made (a module header comment, a test that would fail under the
alternative, a doc-comment explaining why a citation was corrected). Onestone's own DESIGN.md
already models this exactly — "Chaos Six is a Ramsey-inspired tuning constant, not a computed
Ramsey result... naming it honestly... rather than claiming it's 'not a tuned number' is the corner
where this doc previously overclaimed" is a recovered ADR with its own correction history stated
plainly. An `ARCHITECTURE.md`'s ADR list should read the same way: decisions, not doctrine: no ADR
here is a mandate for the *next* service to make the same choice, only a record of what *this* one
did and why.

## 10. Quality

The service's actual quality posture, stated in numbers a reader can re-check: test count and pass
rate (run fresh, never copied), what the test suite actually exercises (property tests? fixed
fixtures? both?), and named quality properties the tests encode as invariants rather than examples
— "the pebble game rejects the double-banana graph while accepting a Laman-minimal graph" is a
quality *property*; "level 12 loads" is a quality *example*. Prefer citing the former.

## 11. Risks and technical debt

**A real list, not a disclaimer paragraph.** Every item: what's wrong, where it lives (file/line or
module), and what it would take to fix. Undocumented vendored duplicates, dead code (a module that
exists but nothing imports it — this standard treats an orphaned module as a debt-list item, not a
harmless leftover), unresolved "open question for the owner" items carried forward from a design
doc without an answer, and every place a doc comment already flags its own honesty gap ("the exact
interaction of blockers with blasts... is genuinely underdetermined by DESIGN.md" — onestone's own
`engine.mts` header) belongs here, cited, not re-discovered from scratch.

## 12. Glossary

House-specific terms a newcomer to this one service would not already know, defined once, tersely.
Omit if the service introduces no vocabulary beyond terms already defined in `DESIGN.md` or this
standard.

## 13. Theory binding (house-specific)

**Which `@lenticule-science/metrologic` object does this game's mechanics actually instantiate — cited to real
files, not asserted by analogy.** This section exists because the owner is explicit that part of
what these games are doing is exploring a new mathematical system (Obsmetrologia) honestly, and the
house has already been burned once by an overclaim in exactly this section (onestone's original
"graph homomorphism" framing for its rejection-sampled fill, corrected in its own DESIGN.md to say
plainly what the check actually enforces). The required shape, following `equivo-design.md`'s own
"What's load-bearing vs. flavor" disclosure convention:

1. **Name the exact package and function** (`@lenticule-science/metrologic/obstruction/cochain.mts`'s
   `cohomologyOfRelation`, `@lenticule-science/metrologic/bilattice`'s `settle`) the mechanic calls, or would
   call if built. If nothing in the game actually calls the math — it only borrows a name or an
   aesthetic — say so in exactly those words. A name borrowed honestly (onestone's Ramsey-inspired
   Chaos Six threshold, disclosed as tuned, not computed) is legitimate flavor; a name borrowed
   silently is the failure mode this section exists to prevent.
2. **State the evidence strength per claim**, following `equivo-design.md` §5-6's per-row labeling
   (Strong / Weakest / corpus-attested / single-document) rather than a single blanket "the math is
   real" assertion covering every mechanic in the service uniformly — a service can have some
   mechanics genuinely load-bearing and others honestly flavor-only in the same document, and both
   are legitimate as long as each is labeled correctly.
3. **Cite a worked example if one exists** — a real invocation of the math function with real
   printed output, per `equivo-design.md` §5's three worked examples (each one states the exact
   command run and the exact output, including one honest surprise the run itself surfaced,
   "kept rather than cleaned up," as evidence the example was actually run and not authored to a
   pre-decided answer).

Omit this section entirely for a service with no math binding to disclose (a pure UI/storefront
service like `play.561.group`) — do not fill it with "not applicable," which is filler; simply do
not include the heading.

## 14. Ludics (house-specific)

What the game is doing as *play*, each claim tied to evidence rather than asserted from genre
convention:

- **Core loop.** The one-sentence loop (swap → match → cascade → settle; click → idle → automate →
  strategize; move → replay → verify → settle), traced to the module that actually implements each
  stage — this is §6's runtime view, read as a play loop rather than a call sequence.
- **Skill expression.** What separates a better player's outcome from a worse one, and where that
  lives in the code — onestone's rigidity-percolation difficulty ramp (§ theory binding) *is* one
  answer; flickering-delve's strategy-editor Lisp program *is* a different, orthogonal one (skill
  expressed as programming, not reflexes). A service with no real skill-expression axis yet (a pure
  idle clicker with no meaningful choice) should say that plainly, per `fleet-definition-of-done.md`'s
  own house standard that a claimed test count or a claimed feature must be one that's actually
  true.
- **Session shape.** Bounded (a level, a daily seed, a run to permadeath) or unbounded (an idle
  game's always-running cascade) — and what that implies for the retention surfaces below. A
  bounded-session game and an unbounded one need structurally different kind-retention mechanics,
  and conflating them is a common design-doc failure mode this section exists to catch early.
- **Retention surfaces, each disclosed by what's real vs. cosmetic**, following the platform
  document's own three-way split (`self-education-platform-design.md` §7's SRS-real /
  drills-real-math-flavor-framing / streaks-cosmetic-only pattern, generalized): name every
  retention mechanic the service ships or plans, and for each one state plainly whether it's a real
  scheduling/mastery system, a real mechanic wearing flavor language, or pure cosmetic
  encouragement with zero effect on scoring or access.
- **Kind-design constraints, stated as refusals, not aspirations.** The house no-list — no
  energy/lives gate that fully blocks free play, no rewarded ads, no streak-loss shaming copy, no
  dark-pattern pinch points, transparent odds wherever chance exists, and (onestone's own naming of
  the sharpest version of this rule) never a level-solvability shortcut sold for money, since
  solvability is a validated mathematical property of the content and selling around it would
  falsify the game's own claims about itself. State which of these constraints this specific
  service enforces via a test (the strongest form) versus policy-only (weaker, and should be named
  as a debt-list item in §11 if a test doesn't yet exist to catch a regression).

## Roadmap appendix format

Every `ARCHITECTURE.md` ends with a roadmap in this exact three-tier shape, and every item in every
tier is **falsifiable** — phrased so that a reader could look at the code in three months and say
definitively whether it happened, never a vibe ("make it more fun") or an open-ended aspiration
("explore multiplayer"):

- **Now** — shipped and verified as of this document's writing (a claim with a test count or a
  passing suite behind it).
- **Next** — scoped, buildable from what exists today with no new design decision required (the
  cartridge/energy-bank wrapper work is the fleet's clearest current example: "wrap existing
  `ledger.mts` behind `EnergyHooks`" is falsifiable and requires no new design).
- **Later** — genuinely blocked on a decision, a dependency that doesn't exist yet, or content that
  hasn't been authored (Equivo's own MVP cut is the house model for how to write this honestly:
  "blocked on owner-authored source material that does not exist in any surveyed corpus" is a real
  later-tier item, not a hedge).

A roadmap item that cannot be falsified — that has no code state, test result, or authored artifact
that would prove it done — does not belong in this appendix. It belongs, if anywhere, in a design
doc's "open questions for the owner" section, which is a different, legitimate, and differently-named
thing.

rooms.title: If the Studios Survived
rooms.description: Owner counterfactual, 2026-08-19: what would Sierra, Impressions, LucasArts, and Rocket Science actually make if each survived to 2026, reasoned from their design values rather than their brands — and which of those hypothetical 2026 games the 561 estate is already, accidentally, building.
rooms.body:
# If the Studios Survived

Owner's question (`sierra-lucasarts-lineage-brief.md` §4): "what if these studios survived
through to today: what would they make?" Answered the way `the-suite-and-the-studio.md`
answered the CD-suite question — strip the brand, keep the design **values**, apply 2026
reasoning (browser-first, live determinism, replay verification, ad-revenue-share economics,
AI players as peers), and see what falls out. Not nostalgia projects. Each section below: the
studio's real values (cited to the research digest), the 2026 game those values produce, then
the honest answer on whether the 561 estate is already building it.

## Sierra On-Line — consequence and death as simulation depth under an adventure skin

**The value, not the brand.** Sierra's actual design signature across King's Quest, Space
Quest, Police Quest, and Phantasmagoria was never "point-and-click" as a genre label — it was
**a willingness to let the world simulate consequences the player didn't ask for**, including
lethal ones, inside a genre everyone else was making safe. Death was real, sudden, often unfair
by modern design standards, and that unfairness was the point: it signaled the world had rules
independent of the protagonist's plot armor. Police Quest additionally fused that with
procedural realism (an ex-cop designer encoding real procedure as the actual puzzle content, not
flavor). The Colonel's Bequest went further: NPCs ran on real-time schedules independent of the
player, so the mystery was a simulation the player observed rather than a script the player
triggered.

**What 2026 Sierra would build.** Not a death-heavy adventure game — that mechanic reads as
cruel-for-its-own-sake to a 2026 audience and Sierra's own later titles already retreated from
it. What survives is the *values*, translated: a world with **real, checkable, non-scripted
consequence** — state that evolves on its own clock, whether or not the player is watching, and
where an accusation, a choice, or a delay can genuinely fail, not fail-and-retry. 2026 Sierra
would build this on a deterministic engine with an intent log specifically *because* that's the
only honest way to guarantee "the world kept moving while you weren't looking" isn't a lie the
designer is telling — replay verification is what makes unscripted consequence trustworthy
rather than arbitrary.

**Is the estate already building it?** Yes, twice, by name. `farstone-qbn-design.md`'s
Building Permit #23 is a quality settling to ⊤ **nobody scripted** — the exact Colonel's-Bequest
shape (a world-clock-derived state resolving on its own) already proven in this codebase, not
hypothesized. And the point-and-click mystery gap (`revivals-anvil-obsidian-mystery.md` §3,
owner-named, ranked #1 in the research digest) is the direct 2026-Sierra answer: real-time
schedules, append-only evidence, an accusation that can honestly fail as "insufficient" rather
than "wrong." It is a planned design, not shipped code — see `planned/mystery-adventure.md`.

## Impressions Games — readable economies and scenario craft, not walker nostalgia

**The value, not the brand.** Impressions' walker model (Part 4 of the research digest) is
often read as the whole point of Caesar/Pharaoh/Zeus, but the walker abstraction was a *means*,
chosen because it made an economy legible at a glance — you could watch the actor walk and
understand your city's service coverage without reading a spreadsheet. The other real value,
separable from the walker mechanic itself, was **scenario craft**: finite, hand-authored
missions with distinct win conditions and a campaign arc moving through history, which taught
the player a widening rule-set one bounded lesson at a time rather than dumping the whole
simulation on them at once.

**What 2026 Impressions would build.** Not a walker-economy clone — the walker's own real
limitations (pathfinding randomness read as frustrating, limited player agency over
distribution, no real material physics, per the digest's Part 4) are well-documented, and a 2026
studio with better simulation tools available would not choose the abstraction that exists
because 1990s hardware couldn't afford real material flow. It would keep the *legibility*
(watch the state, understand the system) and the *scenario/campaign structure* (finite missions,
widening rules, a history to move through), but replace the walker's fixed-throughput
abstraction with real seasonal material chains and survival pressure — exactly the Dawn-of-Man
half of the brief's own instruction (research digest Part 4: "campaign/scenario structure and
resource-loop substance are separable design axes... borrowing scenario shape from one and
resource physics from the other is not a category error").

**Is the estate already building it?** Yes — this is the flagship of the whole wave, already a
full design brief: `seasons-builder-design.md` (working title "Seasonal Round"), Impressions-
style finite scenarios and campaign structure fused with Dawn-of-Man material/seasonal
resource management, first campaign Lakota. See `planned/seasons-builder.md`. Zero code yet, but
design judgment — the actual scarce resource per `the-suite-and-the-studio.md` §4.1 — is spent.

## LucasArts — no-death comedy and cinematic staging, puzzles as jokes with rules

**The value, not the brand.** LucasArts' defining break from Sierra was philosophical, not
technical: Ron Gilbert's design manifesto against arbitrary death and unwinnable states meant
the SCUMM-era games (Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle, Grim Fandango) treated failure
differently — you could not lose the game to a moment you didn't understand was dangerous. The
puzzle was the entire adversarial layer; comedy timing and cinematic staging (camera cuts,
scripted set-pieces, character-driven jokes) did the emotional work a Sierra death-scare would
have done. This is the inverse design value of Sierra's, not a competing flavor of the same
thing — Sierra trusted the world to punish you; LucasArts trusted the world to entertain you
while never punishing you unfairly.

**What 2026 LucasArts would build.** A puzzle-comedy engine where the puzzle **is** the joke —
mechanically fair, generously clued, and staged with real production value (timing, character
voice, visual gags), built to be *finished* and *replayed for delight* rather than beaten once
and shelved. In 2026 terms: no permadeath, no punishing state, a state machine whose failure mode
is "you haven't found the funny solution yet," not "you're locked out." Daily-seeded content
would be a genuinely novel extension LucasArts never had the infrastructure for — a new joke-
puzzle arrangement each day, same cast, same fairness contract every time.

**Is the estate already building it?** Not yet, and this is the honest gap. The point-and-click
mystery gap borrows LucasArts' *engine shape* (state machine, real-time or logic-driven
resolution) but not its *comedy-and-no-death* register — Colonel's Bequest is a Sierra shape
(death is real, the world doesn't care about you), not a LucasArts one. Nothing currently planned
in the estate targets a pure no-death comedy adventure. This is worth naming as the second
adventure-engine build once the mystery chassis exists, not a currently-planned item — flagged
here rather than invented a stub for, per the standing discipline against fabricating scope.

## Rocket Science Games (Obsidian) — place-as-puzzle, the world as the mind

**The value, not the brand.** Rocket Science only shipped one title of real consequence, but
Obsidian's actual design value (research digest Part 6) was distinct even from Myst, its nearest
genre-sibling: where Myst's worlds were book-lore (someone else's story you excavate), Obsidian's
worlds were **externalized cognition** — literal dreams, and an AI's attempt to model its own
nature by building a place. The puzzle-worlds weren't set dressing around puzzles; they were the
puzzle-solver's mind made walkable. Production process matched: art proposed a place freely
("anything can go in a dream"), and puzzle and story were built to fit whatever the place
suggested — an inverted pipeline (place first, puzzle and story after) rather than
story-then-puzzle.

**What 2026 Rocket Science would build.** A slow, first-person, painterly puzzle game where a
real cognitive or logical system is not represented by the puzzles but **is** the puzzles — no
translation layer between "the math" and "the content." 2026 gives this studio something 1996
Rocket Science didn't have: an actual house-owned formal system (obstruction/settling,
four-valued logic) to build the dream-worlds *out of*, rather than inventing dream-logic puzzles
from whole cloth the way the original had to.

**Is the estate already building it?** Yes, as a planned design: `revivals-anvil-obsidian-
mystery.md` §2, the Obsidian-lineage AI Myst-like, where `@lenticule-science/metrologic`'s obstruction engine
(already load-bearing in Crucible) and the abrash/durante-proven four-valued readout supply real
puzzle content with, per the design note's own claim, "zero translation." See
`planned/obsidian-lineage.md`. Also unbuilt, design-only — and the note names Obsidian's own
commercial failure as a real, unsoftened risk, not a hypothetical one.

## What this counterfactual is missing on purpose

No studio row for Dynamix (flight/sports sim) or the pure-arcade LucasArts early titles
(Rescue on Fractalus!, Ballblazer) — neither has an owner-named signal or a values argument this
document can make honestly without inventing one. The Anvil-of-Dawn/DreamForge lineage (grid
dungeon crawler, tempo-controlled combat, no-XP skill-by-use) is deliberately not framed as a
"what would the studio build in 2026" counterfactual here, because DreamForge's actual design
value — tight single-hero combat feel — is a craft property, not a values argument the way the
other four studios' choices were; it belongs with the revivals note as a chassis to build, not
a counterfactual to reason through. See `planned/extraction-crawler.md` for that one; it is the
fourth planned note in this wave but sits outside this document's "values, not brand" frame on
purpose.

## Sources

`sierra-lucasarts-lineage-brief.md` §4 (the owner's question, verbatim); the research digest
Parts 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 (catalog and mechanical detail, cited inline above); `seasons-builder-
design.md` and `revivals-anvil-obsidian-mystery.md` (the estate's actual planned answers, read
directly this session, both already-existing design documents, not summarized from memory);
`the-suite-and-the-studio.md` §4.1 (design judgment as the scarce resource, load-bearing for the
LucasArts-gap paragraph's framing).

rooms.title: Naming the Three Houses
rooms.description: Sub-brand naming pass, superseding Three Marks' use of the parent names as section brands: candidate names with market reasoning for the public games label (cutesy indie under Causeway), the game-systems brand (Valve/Microsoft register under Red Cup), and the game-sciences brand (ludics register under Lenticule). Shortlists + one recommendation each; owner decides.
rooms.body:
# Naming the Three Houses

Correction to [Three Marks](three-marks-branding.md): the owner wants **new names** for
these three sections — the parents (Causeway Services, Red Cup Engineering, Lenticule
Science) stay as the section-tree brands, and each services-section may name its own
brand; these three deserve it. Three Marks' *architecture* survives unchanged (audience
separation, the colophon rule, namespaces-are-filing); only the names at the gaming level
are new. The feeling-rule I'm meeting: each parent name is a plain physical thing whose
function quietly describes its section. The sub-brands below hold that rule while hitting
each market's native register.

## 1. The games label — cutesy indie register (under Causeway)

**Market reality:** the labels that win here are warm, short, mascot-capable, and read
instantly on a browser tab: PopCap, Finji, Panic/Playdate, Coolmath's sheer memorability.
Casual/browser players bookmark a *creature or object*, not an abstraction. Our fit
constraints: coastal/water estate motifs, the earn-only economy as identity, favicon-first.

**Recommended: COWRIE** (Cowrie Games). A cowrie is a small, glossy, instantly-drawable
seashell — *and cowries were real money across half the world for centuries.* A currency
that is also a cute shell is our earn-only economy ("we pay you") compressed into one
image a player can hold. Shells also rhyme with what the shelf technically is — games in
one shared shell (chrome/cartridge). Mascot, favicon, and name are the same object.
Conflict scan: an open-source SSH honeypot uses the name in security tooling — different
market entirely, low collision risk; no notable game-industry use found.

**Runners-up:**
- **Pebble Otter** — sea otters keep a favorite pebble in a pouch to crack shells:
  stones + sea + play, the entire estate in one animal, and the single most mascot-able
  option. Two words is its only weakness; "Pebble" alone is trademark-encumbered (watches).
- **Periwinkle** — beach snail AND a friendly color; extremely cute; weaker meaning-load
  than Cowrie (no economy story).
- **Spindrift** — sea-spray; beautiful, light; already a sparkling-water brand (crowded).
- Rejected with reason: **Sand Dollar** (it's literally the Bahamas' CBDC — a real
  currency conflict, not just a trademark one); **Tidepool** (already a game of ours);
  **Sandcastle** (the image is impermanence — anti-thesis of the finished-games shelf).

## 2. The game-systems brand — Valve/Microsoft register (under Red Cup)

**Market reality:** engine brands that command respect are one hard noun with industrial
or craft weight — Valve, Source, Unreal, Havok, RAD. The name should make a developer
assume load-bearing seriousness before reading a line of docs. Our fit constraints:
zero-dependency composition, contracts as the only coupling, determinism, the vessel/kiln
family resemblance to Red Cup.

**Recommended: DRYSTONE** (Drystone — "a Drystone system"). Drystone walling is the craft
of building walls from fitted stones with **no mortar** — structures that stand for
centuries held by nothing but how precisely the pieces fit. That is the house engineering
doctrine stated as a craft: no mortar = zero dependencies; held by fit = coupled only by
contract. It carries Valve-like gravitas, it's visually brandable (a coursed wall), it
quietly shares the stone motif with the public estate without being matchy, and
"Drystone replay verifier / Drystone cartridge" all sound inevitable. Conflict scan: no
notable game-tech use found; masonry firms only.

**Runners-up:**
- **Kiln** — the oven that fires vessels: the literal parent-link (a kiln is what makes
  red cups), warm-industrial, four letters. Slight softness next to Drystone; a defunct
  Fog Creek source-control product once used it (dead, low risk).
- **Ashlar** — precision-dressed building stone; the engineered stone to Causeway's
  walked stone; more obscure, which cuts both ways.
- **Bellows** — feeds the fire (pairs beautifully with Stoke); more component than
  institution.
- Rejected with reason: **Weir** (Weir Group plc is a major real engineering firm),
  **Dovetail** (Dovetail Games exists), **Foundry** (Foundry VTT), **Keystone** (generic,
  heavily used across software).

## 3. The game-sciences brand — ludics register (under Lenticule)

**Market reality:** the institutions people cite with affection are lab-with-soul names —
Santa Fe Institute, Bell Labs — or a single resonant term of art. Game studies' own
vocabulary is rich and mostly unclaimed as brands. Our fit constraint is unusual: the
house *proved* a mapping from Caillois's play categories onto its settling regimes, so a
Caillois term here isn't decoration — it's the lab named for its own theorem.

**Recommended: ILINX** (Ilinx — "an Ilinx working paper"). Ilinx is Caillois's fourth and
strangest category: vertigo, the play of losing stable ground. In the house mapping it is
the H¹ ≠ 0 regime — the *unsettleable* — which is precisely the frontier the science
section actually studies (obstruction, contradiction held as situation, the edge past
settled knowledge). Five letters, striking, pleasant to say, essentially unclaimed in the
market. A research brand named for the vertigo it investigates meets Lenticule's
lens-rule and beats it for nerve. Conflict scan: appears occasionally in game-studies
journal prose (which is a feature — the field will get it instantly); no significant
commercial holder found.

**Runners-up:**
- **Paidia** — Caillois's free-play pole; warmer and more welcoming than Ilinx; loses
  the on-theorem edge (the house's proved regimes light up Ilinx specifically).
- **Astragal** — the knucklebone die (oldest randomizer in archaeology) AND an
  architectural molding: chance + structure in one obscure-but-learnable word.
- **Alea** — chance itself; pretty; diluted by broad prior use (alea iacta est,
  AleaSoft, journal names).
- Rejected with reason: **Ludens** (Kojima Productions' mascot), **Knucklebones**
  (a prominent Cult of the Lamb minigame), **Magic Circle** (generic within the field),
  **Winter Count** (reserved: Lakota material belongs to the campaign under its own
  discipline, not to a lab wordmark — owner's call alone).

## 4. The set, together

**Cowrie · Drystone · Ilinx** — a shell on the shore, a wall above it, a whirlpool past
it. Coastal without matching, three registers without dissonance, and each one carries
its section's actual thesis: a currency-shell for the earn-only shelf, mortarless masonry
for zero-dependency contracts, named vertigo for the study of the unsettleable. Colophon
form under the Three Marks rule: *"A Cowrie game · Drystone systems · Ilinx mathematics."*

Alternate coherent set if the owner wants maximum-cute up front: **Pebble Otter · Kiln ·
Paidia** (the otter cracks shells on a stone; the kiln fires the cup; paidia is the play
that needs no rules). Softer everywhere; less thesis-per-name.

All decisions the owner's; nothing here has been applied to any artifact yet.

rooms.title: Durante
rooms.description: Stub note for Durante, a first-playable Quake-like FPS built on the abrash raycaster engine — built in the legacy archive, a recovery candidate, not an unbuilt concept. The owner's correction honored directly: shooters are not unbuilt.
rooms.body:
# Durante

**Status: built in legacy archive — recovery candidate.** This is the owner's correction, honored
directly: **shooters are not unbuilt.** Durante is a real, first-playable Quake-like FPS that was
built and (per its own README) tested — "walk a level, strafe, shoot a demon" — not an absent
concept waiting for a first design pass.

## What was actually built

A software-rendered first-person shooter on top of `@561-group/abrash` (the raycaster engine — see
`render-substrate-service`'s note). Its README claims 62 assertions across 4 proof files (arena,
demon, combat, game). It is genuinely first-playable, not a tech demo: a level to walk, strafing
movement, a demon to fight.

## Where it actually lives (pointers, not copies)

1. **The read-only archive copy** —
   `561-group/lib/legacy/2026-08-17-vps-561-group/_archive/from-content-source/apps/games/durante`.
   62 assertions / 4 proofs claimed by its README; **unverifiable as claimed** — `tests/` in this
   copy holds only `_harness.mjs`, the 4 named proof files (`arena`, `demon`, `combat`, `game`) are
   absent.
2. **Two further broken snapshot copies**, already sitting in the *active* tree at
   `public-services-section/.../public-computer-games-services-section/services/durante-services-section/lib/legacy/{2026-06-17-durante,2026-08-17-windows-561-group-apps-games-durante}`.
   Both copies' `package.json` test scripts point at `tests/arena.test.mjs`,
   `combat.test.mjs`, `demon.test.mjs`, `game.test.mjs` — but both copies' `tests/` directories
   contain only `_harness.mjs`. `npm test` was run on both this session (not protected — these are
   duplicate legacy copies inside an already-public services tree, not the read-only archive) and
   both fail immediately with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. The active `durante-services-section` directory
   itself has **no live top-level app** — only these two broken copies.

## Recovery against the active tree

**Durante rides abrash, which rides daleske.** Recovering a playable Durante means, in order:
1. Recover `render-substrate-service`'s stack first — specifically daleske (the pixel/raster
   terminal framework Durante's engine renders through) and abrash (the raycaster game engine
   Durante is built on). Neither game logic nor the render layer can come back independently.
2. Reconstruct or re-author the 4 missing proof files (`arena`, `demon`, `combat`, `game`) — none
   of the three copies on disk (the archive original or either active-tree snapshot) has them, so
   "recovery" here means re-deriving test coverage from the surviving `src/`, not restoring an
   existing proof set.
3. Only then would a `npm test` run against a real, checkable Durante be possible — as of this
   note, no copy of Durante anywhere in the tree has a working test suite.

## Sources

Task orchestrator's built-asset inventory §7 and §8 (games/durante); this workflow's own disk
verification (`npm test` run on both active-tree copies, both failing `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`;
proof-file presence checked in the archive copy, absent).

## Staircase tier

Not on the planned-game staircase — this is a recovery item, not a design-stage item. The
work required is engineering recovery (rebuild the render stack, re-derive tests), not design
judgment.

rooms.title: Energy Tiling
rooms.description: Stub note for the energy-tiling shared-board game ('r/place but bejeweled,' the windy hinterlands) — a planned single shared-world tile board where transforming a tile costs energy scaled by move complexity and skill. Status: planned — no code exists.
rooms.body:
# Energy Tiling ("r/place but bejeweled," the windy hinterlands)

**Status: planned — no code exists.** No service, no board implementation. Crucible
(`public-web-game-services-section/services/crucible-service`, in-build) is the piloted
solo-scale precursor to this game's cost mechanic — it is a real, separate, in-build service, not
this game under a different name.

## Concept

One shared board — not per-player instances — where tiling or transforming a cell costs energy
scaled by move complexity and the player's own skill. New players start in the "windy
hinterlands," the periphery of the one shared world, and the game is social from the start:
players can pool and sell energy to each other. The aesthetic is pitched as "weird Flatlander meets
weird Zachtronics." The open design question, stated explicitly in the source note rather than
glossed over: how does energy accrue at all — the note does not yet answer this.

## Sources

- `gaming-enterprises-vision.md` §2 (whole section).
- `fleet-spec-coverage-and-roadmap.md` — roadmap "Later" tier.
- Crucible's own design documents (`crucible-service/DESIGN.md`), which pilot this game's cost
  mechanic at solo scale using the real `@lenticule-science/metrologic` obstruction/cohomology engine — read
  those for the actual, currently-running version of the underlying cost math.

## Staircase tier

**Later**, piloted at Next-tier scale via Crucible. The shared-board version itself is not
scheduled; Crucible's solo-scale build is the concrete, in-build proxy for validating the cost
mechanic before any shared board is attempted.

## Smallest first step

Answer the open design question the vision note itself leaves unresolved — how energy accrues on
a shared board with no single player's session to gate it — before any code is written. That
answer is a design decision, not an engineering task, and per house roadmap discipline a step this
document cannot make falsifiable belongs here as a named blocker, not as invented scope.

rooms.title: Equivo
rooms.description: Stub note for Equivo, 'Duolingo for mathematics' — a planned self-education game teaching how to observe equivalence by measuring obstruction, riding real @lenticule-science/metrologic bilattice/obstruction code. Status: planned — no code exists.
rooms.body:
# Equivo

**Status: planned — no code exists.** No service, no lesson corpus, no `equivo-service` package
anywhere in the tree. The checker math it would call is real and already runs (see below); the
game built on top of it is not.

## Concept

"Duolingo for mathematics," teaching a player to observe equivalence by measuring obstruction
rather than by rote symbol manipulation. The learner runs a real four-stage descent —
**articulate → predicate → posit → settle** — against `@lenticule-science/metrologic`'s actual bilattice and
obstruction code, not a simulated approximation of it. Six exercise types are specified
(distinguish / relate / measure / settle / observe / repair) across four presentation-register
lenses (obsmetrologia, semiotics, relationality, and an honestly-absent Lakotaean lens pending
owner-authored source material that does not yet exist). It rides the same Self-Education Platform
chassis Lantern already substantially is.

## Sources

- `equivo-design.md` — the whole document; three worked examples are run against real
  `@lenticule-science/metrologic` code in §5, each with the exact command and exact output printed, including one
  honest surprise the run itself surfaced.
- `self-education-platform-design.md` — the shared chassis (corpus-compiler, FSRS-lite SRS,
  pluggable `Checker` interface, two-part mastery model) Equivo would ride.
- `wilder-conceptions-01.md` items 1–2, 5 — cross-references to the Carrier Audit discipline and
  the `regime`-field proposal, both relevant to how Equivo would disclose its own mechanics.

## Staircase tier

**Later.** The design's own MVP cut explicitly defers Type F exercises, the Lakotaean register,
and the lesson corpus itself, each with a named blocking reason — none a scheduling matter a
roadmap can shrink. This is not "not yet scheduled," it is "blocked on content that doesn't exist."

## Smallest first step

Author one real lesson (one worked descent: articulate → predicate → posit → settle) for a single
concrete equivalence claim, run entirely against real `@lenticule-science/metrologic` code with printed output —
the same discipline `equivo-design.md` §5's three worked examples already model — before writing
any `Checker` interface code. The blocking resource is one authored lesson, not one line of
infrastructure; the platform chassis it would run on (Lantern's five modules) already exists.

rooms.title: Extraction Crawler
rooms.description: Stub note for the Anvil-of-Dawn-lineage browser extraction crawler — blockstep grid movement, tempo-controlled combat, no-XP skill-by-use, ported (not literally revived) from the house-owned abrash/durante substrate. Status: planned-design-note-exists — full chassis design written, zero code.
rooms.body:
# Extraction Crawler

**Status: planned-design-note-exists.** A compact chassis design exists
(`revivals-anvil-obsidian-mystery.md` §1, in this same `notes/` directory). No game code
exists for this game specifically; it draws on but does not reuse the runtime of two related,
already-built legacy modules (see below).

## Concept

A browser first-person grid dungeon crawler in the Anvil of Dawn / Dungeon Master movement
register: discrete cells, 90-degree turns, no free-look ("blockstep" navigation, not
continuous 3D movement). Stakes are extraction, not clearance — descend, grab what you can
carry, exit alive with the haul or lose the run. Reads the owner's "almost DOOM but...
excursion shooters" (`sierra-lucasarts-lineage-brief.md` §3, likely "extraction" shooters) as
extraction, matching the research digest's own framing.

## Why the house can do it — and the honest revival judgment

Two real, tested legacy modules exist, read directly this session:

- `@561-group/abrash` — a software raycaster (grid-DDA) over a federated voxel world, four-
  valued solidity readout (t/f/⊥/⊤, with ⊤ rendered as a designed "shivering" contested-wall
  effect, not a bug), pure and deterministic per its own README (81 assertions / 5 proofs
  claimed). See `planned/render-substrate.md` for this module's own status and recovery
  notes.
- `@561-group/durante` — a first-playable Quake-like built on abrash (62 assertions / 4 proofs
  claimed). See `planned/durante.md` for this module's own status as a **recovery candidate**,
  distinct from this game.

**Neither module targets a browser** — both render into `@561-group/daleske`, a terminal
kitty/sixel pixel framework. The design note's explicit, honest verdict: a literal revival
(running the terminal renderer, shipping it as `<game>.561.group`) does not serve a
browser-first product. What is worth reviving is the *design discipline* — the pure
vec2/rotation kernel, the DDA raycaster with zero hidden nondeterminism, the four-valued
world-as-fold model, and the proven fact that a contested wall as a designed mechanic already
plays today. The recommended path is a **fresh Canvas 2D raycaster that ports abrash's math
and four-valued readout discipline verbatim**, not a runtime resurrection.

## Core loop

Single-hero, tempo-controlled combat (attacking fast speeds up the enemy's attack rate;
attacking slow slows it — Anvil of Dawn's own most distinctive and most critically-praised
mechanic), no XP — skill-by-use instead, the same pattern Farstone already uses. Contested
(⊤) walls are a real in-fiction hazard, not a bug.

## Staircase tier

**Next**, alongside the energy-tiling hinterlands — pairs with ruinfold's Deep-shelf daily
ritual once the extraction-loss stakes have somewhere real to settle (the Energy Bank, itself
still a Fable proposal, not built).

## Honest risks (named in the design note, not softened here)

1. Blockstep movement is a genuine period taste — may read as deliberately retro rather than
   fresh, a framing risk more than a technical one.
2. "Lose the run's haul" needs a real stakes economy to mean anything, and the Energy Bank
   that would carry that stake is a proposal only, not built.
3. Anvil's tempo-controlled combat is the hardest single mechanic to get right — a feel/balance
   problem, not a determinism problem; the source material's own critical praise singles out
   exactly this system as the hard part to nail.

## Sources

`sierra-lucasarts-lineage-brief.md` §3 (owner statement, verbatim); `revivals-anvil-obsidian-
mystery.md` §1 (the full chassis design, same directory); `planned/render-substrate.md` and
`planned/durante.md` (the related legacy-recovery stubs this design explicitly does not
reuse as runtime); `if-the-studios-survived.md` (notes this game as a craft-value chassis
rather than a studio-values counterfactual, on purpose).

## Smallest first step

Port the abrash one-room proving-ground demo to Canvas 2D and prove bit-identical replay —
before any dungeon content, combat tuning, or extraction-stakes economy is authored.

# Farstone Service Note

**Status: built as legacy MUD (read-only archive); QBN redesign specified, no active code yet.**

## Concept

Farstone names two real artifacts sharing a common ancestor, not one town in two formats. **The
pyfars polity** is an in-fiction municipality — Mayor Aliyah Reyes, Harbormaster Takeshi Aoki, city
hall, a permit backlog aging past its 30-day charter window — authored as markdown-plus-frontmatter
governance records that a Python engine (pyfars) dispatches work against. **`@561-group/farstone`**
is a *built*, playable MUD — JavaScript game content riding the `tab` EAVT world-engine and the
FizzOS MUD driver, servable over HTTP/SSE and playable in a browser today — whose seed-island world
carries the same Takeshi Aoki (verbatim-matching biography) and the same eleven place-slugs as the
pyfars polity, and whose headline mechanic is that Building Permit #23 ages under its own clock past
its decision window and settles to a bilattice ⊤ (held contradiction) with no scripted "permits go
bad" rule — the fold produces it. That mechanic is already storylet-shaped: a quality settling to a
value nobody scripted, surfaced as content. A QBN redesign would keep both artifacts as content wells
(pyfars for governance-record texture and the permit/office/duty convention; the legacy MUD for room
prose, NPC bios, and the needs/mood loop) while building new game logic against the *current*,
actively-tested FizzOS package rather than the retired tab-riding lineage the legacy MUD actually
depends on.

## Pointers

- Design note (verdict, core loop, content pipeline, qualities, prose-at-volume risk, staircase
  placement, cast, load-bearing disclosure):
  `services/561-group-gaming-enterprises-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/farstone-qbn-design.md`
- Legacy MUD (built, playable, read-only reference — do not treat as the target runtime):
  `lib/legacy/2026-08-17-vps-561-group/_archive/from-content-source/apps/games/farstone/`
  (four content packs: `farstone/` seed island, `farstone-harbor/` the served ~30-room world,
  `farstone-tale/` designed DSL world, `farstone-wild/` generated world; depends on the retired
  `@561-group/tab` + old `@561-group/fizzos` lineage, per its own README)
- pyfars governance polity (records, not runtime — the fiction-vs-deployment discriminator applies):
  `lib/legacy/2026-08-17-vps-561-group/_archive/code/pyfars/examples/farstone/`
- Active FizzOS engine (the real target for any new build; 60/60 tests, one dependency —
  `@lenticule-science/metrologic`, no `tab` import):
  `services/computer-services-section/services/computer-systems-services-section/services/computer-mud-services-section/apps/fizzos/`

## Smallest first step

Re-author Permit #23's ages-into-⊤ arc — the one piece of content proven twice, by two different
authoring passes, in two different engines — as three or four cells against the *active* fizzos's
`predication.mjs` / `world-clock.mjs` (a `within-window` predicate, its declared converse, one
tick-boundary rule), render it through a bare page reading the assertions trace, and confirm it
settles to a visibly-contradictory state on its own after N ticks with zero hand-written "if
overdue" branch. That proves the thesis in the smallest possible unit, on the engine that is
actually alive today.

# Fyreside

**Status: dormant — a single orphaned source fragment, not a built game.** This note flags a
discrepancy up front rather than papering over it: the task orchestrator that requested this stub
grouped fyreside with durante, the render substrate, wheatstone, and okaga under one status label
("built in legacy archive — recovery candidate"). What's actually on disk does not support that
label, and this note states what's true instead — per this workflow's standing instruction to
verify every status claim on disk, that instruction overrides the suggested phrasing where the two
disagree.

## What's actually there

The active `fyreside-services-section` directory
(`public-services-section/.../public-computer-games-services-section/services/fyreside-services-section/lib/legacy/cards.py`)
holds exactly one file: a single Python `Card` base class. No game loop, no `package.json`, no
tests, no README anywhere in the section. This is not comparable to the other four legacy stubs in
this section, each of which is a complete (if now-broken or proof-stripped) application with a
package.json, a `src/` tree, and at least a claimed test suite — durante and okaga are archived
*games*; wheatstone and the render substrate are archived, proof-file-backed *engines*. Fyreside is
one class.

It also lives in a different place than the other four: durante/render-substrate/wheatstone/okaga
all sit in the read-only `_archive/from-content-source/` tree; fyreside's fragment sits directly in
the *active* tree's own `lib/legacy/`, one directory below a section that has otherwise never held
a working build.

## Concept (as far as the fragment states one)

A card-game seed — the `Card` class's shape (whatever fields/methods it defines) is the only
evidence of design intent that exists; no rules, no game loop, no variant is specified anywhere in
the surveyed corpus or on disk.

## Recovery against the active tree

There is no working build to "recover" in the sense the other four stubs use that word — recovery
here means authoring a game from a single reusable class, not reconstructing tests around
surviving application logic. The honest first step, if this seed is picked up: read `cards.py` in
full, decide what game (if any) its `Card` shape was heading toward, and treat everything past that
class as a fresh design task rather than a restoration.

## Sources

Task orchestrator's built-asset inventory §7 (fyreside-services-section row: "dormant (source
fragment only)"); this workflow's own disk check of the section's contents.

## Staircase tier

Not applicable in the recovery sense the other four legacy stubs use — this is closer to the
planned-game "no code exists" bucket than to a genuine recovery candidate, except that one file
of prior intent does exist. Not scheduled on any tier in the assigned corpus.

# Gamified Fediverse Client

**Status: planned — no game layer exists.** A real, standards-conformant ActivityPub *server*
already exists and is landed (50/50 tests verified) at
`computer-systems-services-section/services/web-services-section/services/web-protocol-services-section/services/activitypub-services-section` —
that tree is **not** this game and is **not stubbed**, per the in-build/landed-elsewhere rule; this
note only covers the game layer on top of it, which does not exist. A targeted grep found zero
rendering, world-model, or game-loop code anywhere in the four "Semioverse"-named sections in the
corpus.

## Concept

An ActivityPub client that turns the whole public Fediverse network into an MMORPG, seen from one
instance's own perspective — named in the vision note as "the same destination" as the Commons and
the undersea MUD, approached from a third side: agents-as-actors rather than a shared tile board or
a simulated ecology. `wilder-conceptions-01.md` item 6 proposes measuring real federation-delivery
latency between instances and using it as the literal causal-set geometry of Commons regions, once
a live, reachable instance exists to measure latency against.

## Sources

- `gaming-enterprises-vision.md` §5a (whole section).
- `semioverse-state-and-fediverse-client-feasibility.md` (whole document — the feasibility/recon
  pass this stub's status claim is drawn from).
- `wilder-conceptions-01.md` item 6.

## Staircase tier

**Later**, hard-blocked on the deploy step. The ActivityPub server went live as a local devbox
instance same-day (per the ringleader's response: "50/50 tests, signed loopback federation
proven") — but a local devbox instance is not a reachable federation, and the source note itself
names the deploy step as "the smallest honest first step," not a completed one. x402 payments are
conceptually scaffolded in the corpus, not executed anywhere.

## Smallest first step

Deploy the existing ActivityPub server to a reachable public endpoint — the server itself needs no
new code to attempt this, per the feasibility note's own conclusion. Once reachable, logging real
federation-delivery latency as a metric is named as a near-free sub-step that requires no game code
at all, and would be the first real data this game's eventual causal-set-geometry mechanic could be
built against.

rooms.body:
# Mystery Adventure

**Status: planned-design-note-exists.** A compact chassis design exists
(`revivals-anvil-obsidian-mystery.md` §3, in this same `notes/` directory). No game code
exists; no story or case content is written.

## The gap, stated plainly

Nothing point-and-click exists in the estate today. The owner: "I loved those as a kid"
(`sierra-lucasarts-lineage-brief.md` §2). The research digest's catalog audit identifies the
specific mechanical shape worth wanting as not generic point-and-click but **The Colonel's
Bequest / Laura Bow** — a detective-protagonist whodunit built on real-time NPC schedules, not
a fixed dialogue tree. This is the highest-ranked gap in the research digest's ranked list
(#1 of 7).

## Why the house can do it

A mystery's clue graph **is** a state machine with a replayable solution path — natively
intent-loggable and daily-seedable (a new suspect/clue arrangement per seed) in a way arcade
genres are not. This is corroborated directly by `farstone-qbn-design.md`, the house's closest
existing design work to this shape:

- Farstone's Building Permit #23 already demonstrates the exact mechanism a mystery's evidence
  needs: a quality (window-state) settling to a value nobody scripted — the branch is a
  property of the bilattice join, triggered by one binding made once. Evidence that is
  simultaneously alibi-confirmed and alibi-contradicted is not a special case to hand-code; it
  is the same ⊤-state abrash/durante already render as a designed mechanic (see
  `planned/durante.md`, `planned/render-substrate.md`), and Farstone already settles it as a
  storylet.
- Farstone's quality taxonomy (append-only trained stat, decaying need, derived-not-stored,
  contested/⊤-legal, relational, world-clock-derived) maps onto a mystery's own state almost
  without translation: alibi = world-clock-derived, suspect relationships = the relational
  family already committed in Farstone's world data, and — load-bearing — evidence that both
  supports and contradicts a suspect is contested/⊤-legal, a first-class value in the house
  substrate rather than an error state.

## Proposed chassis (no story written)

Built on the current, live **fizzos** substrate (assertions-trace + Belnap-FOUR fold, one
dependency, `@lenticule-science/metrologic`) — not the retired tab/EAVT lineage the old Farstone MUD content
was authored against:

1. Suspects carry schedules as world-clock-derived cells — where a suspect is and what they
   are doing is a pure function of the case's world-clock, not a hand-scripted cutscene per
   hour.
2. Evidence is append-only witnessed fact, gathered the same way abrash/durante append
   predicate/deny evidence.
3. An accusation is a settle-check against the fold, not a multiple-choice pick — evidence
   either settles cleanly to true against one suspect, or exposes the case as legitimately
   ⊤ (contradictory, insufficient), and the game can honestly say "you don't have it yet" as a
   distinct legal state from "wrong suspect."
4. Daily-seeded cases, reusing one engine across many finite, bounded mysteries — matching the
   house's portfolio-economics argument (many small, finished, shared-substrate games beats
   hit-chasing).

## Staircase tier

Owner-named, ranked #1 in the research digest's gap list; naturally sequenced just after or
alongside Farstone's own smallest real step, since both share the live-fizzos substrate and
the assertions-trace/settle mechanism — plausibly the second thing built on that engine, not a
separate initiative. Shelf-wise: The Deep (shared engine kinship with Farstone), though its
player-facing register (bounded, finished mystery cases) is closer to The Puzzle Den's
done-ness contract than to an open MUD.

## Honest risks (named in the design note, not softened here)

1. Prose-at-volume is unproven anywhere in the corpus — a good mystery needs real red
   herrings, suspect dialogue, and alibi text at genuine volume and quality; existing Farstone
   prose is good at small scale (~30 rooms, single-pass), not proven at a mystery's branching,
   quality-gated scale.
2. A fair mystery engine is not the same thing as a good one — misdirection, character, and
   pacing are authorial craft the state machine does not supply on its own; this is the
   design-judgment bottleneck named as the house's actual scarce resource, not an engineering
   problem this chassis solves by existing.

## Sources

`sierra-lucasarts-lineage-brief.md` §2 (owner statement, verbatim); `revivals-anvil-obsidian-
mystery.md` §3 (the full chassis design, same directory); `farstone-qbn-design.md` (the
corroborating mechanism, cited throughout); `if-the-studios-survived.md` (this game's
counterfactual framing — 2026 Sierra's answer, not LucasArts', because the mechanic is
consequence-driven, not no-death comedy).

## Smallest first step

A three-suspect, single-location micro-case: author suspect schedules and a handful of
evidence facts against fizzos's real module surface (`world.mjs`, `predication.mjs`,
`world-clock.mjs`), build the accusation-settle mechanic, and confirm "insufficient evidence"
is honestly distinguishable from "wrong suspect" — before any prose, red herrings, or a real
story are written.

rooms.title: Obsidian Lineage
rooms.description: Stub note for the Obsidian-lineage AI Myst-like — a slow, first-person puzzle game where the house's own obstruction/settling math and four-valued logic are the puzzle content with zero translation, not a reskin. Status: planned-design-note-exists — full chassis design written, zero code.
rooms.body:
# Obsidian Lineage

**Status: planned-design-note-exists.** A compact chassis design exists
(`revivals-anvil-obsidian-mystery.md` §2, in this same `notes/` directory). No game code
exists.

## Concept

A slow, surreal, first-person puzzle game about artificial intelligence, structured like
Obsidian (1996, Rocket Science Games): distinct dream-worlds — two human dreamers, and a
now-sentient orbital AI attempting to model its own cognition — that the player walks through
solving puzzles built literally out of the house's own standing theory: obstruction/settling
and four-valued (Belnap) logic, presented as dream-machine puzzle content rather than
translated into a fictional idiom first. Per the owner directly: "that shit? Seems very up
our alley" (`sierra-lucasarts-lineage-brief.md` §3).

Obsidian's actual theme, per the research digest, is not book-lore like Myst — it is dreams
and the subconscious, worlds that are externalized attempts by an AI to understand its own
nature. That is not a loose analogy to the house's subject matter; it is the same subject
matter, which is why the design note frames this as the one game in the wave where the math
**is** the fiction.

## Why the house can do it

Two real pieces of substrate, already built, not invented for this game:

- `@lenticule-science/metrologic`'s obstruction engine, already load-bearing in Crucible (shipped design):
  assigns a canonical complexity number (H¹ rank, settling depth, regime) to a transformation.
  A puzzle whose difficulty is its obstruction rank is the same computation Crucible already
  runs, aimed at a dream-scene instead of a wallet.
- The bilattice four-value readout (t/f/⊥/⊤) is already proven playable, not just theorized —
  abrash and durante (see `planned/render-substrate.md`, `planned/durante.md`) render ⊤ as a
  designed, shivering, split-tinted mechanic and settle a contested vitality cell as combat's
  actual kill condition.

This should be built SVG-first, not on the abrash/durante raycaster — Obsidian's real pacing
(slow, static, painterly, one scene at a time) fits hand-built or generated SVG scenes, not a
real-time raycaster. It is the SVG-tier sibling of the extraction crawler, not the 3D-tier one.

## Core loop

The player walks a small set of dream-scenes (Obsidian's own three-world structure). Each
scene is a settled or unsettled region of the house's own logic, rendered as a puzzle: an
obstruction puzzle asks the player to find a lower-obstruction path to an equivalent outcome
(the same skill Crucible already teaches); a ⊤-scene asks the player to recognize and hold a
contradiction, or gather the witness that settles it; a ⊥-scene is legitimately unscanned, and
the puzzle is finding what evidence would resolve it at all. The ending, per Obsidian's own
precedent, maps onto a house-native choice: does the fold your play has built settle to
consensus, or stay held open — both real, legal states, not a right/wrong binary dressed as
philosophy.

## Staircase tier

Independent of Crucible, not sequenced behind it — Crucible pilots the obstruction engine as
an economy (move cost); this pilots the identical engine as puzzle content (scene meaning).
Natural home is a new shelf register alongside The Study (weiqi/Lantern/Equivo), given the
shared "the math is the content, not the skin" property, though it is fiction-forward enough
it could equally sit with The Stars once Okaga-scale narrative ambitions are underway.

## Honest risks (named in the design note, not softened here)

1. The "zero translation" pitch risks reading as clever to the house and opaque to a player
   with no reason to know obstruction-rank math exists — a writer's-touch problem
   (`farstone-qbn-design.md` §5's "prose/craft at volume" risk), not a solved one.
2. Obsidian itself is a real cautionary data point: critically loved, commercially dead — its
   failure directly closed Rocket Science Games. The house's earn-only, ad-revenue-share
   economics may sidestep 1996 packaged-goods economics, but that is a hopeful structural
   argument, not a demonstrated one; this genre has failed commercially once before at the
   highest quality bar achievable at the time.

## Sources

`sierra-lucasarts-lineage-brief.md` §3 (owner statement, verbatim); `revivals-anvil-obsidian-

# Okaga

**Status: built in legacy archive — recovery candidate.**

## What was actually built

An Elite-like space-flight game built on tsander (the wireframe-3D engine — see
`render-substrate-service`'s note). Its README explicitly frames it as "a GAME, not just a
setting" — claiming "galaxy + trade + ship + game proofs," though no single explicit assertion
count was found in the source material.

## Where it actually lives (pointer, not a copy)

Read-only archive at
`561-group/lib/legacy/2026-08-17-vps-561-group/_archive/from-content-source/apps/games/okaga`.
**Unverifiable as claimed** — `tests/` in this copy holds only `_harness.mjs`; the galaxy/trade/
ship/game proof files are absent.

## Recovery against the active tree

**Okaga rides tsander**, which rides arnold. Recovering a playable Okaga means recovering
`render-substrate-service`'s stack first — specifically tsander, whose own proof files are also
absent and would need re-deriving from surviving `src/` before Okaga's game logic could be
meaningfully tested. There is no active-tree copy of Okaga anywhere else in the estate to recover
*against*; this archive copy is the only one that exists.

## A separate, later-stage vision item shares this name — recorded here, not conflated

`gaming-enterprises-vision.md` §4 names "Okaga-setting games" as a distinct, vision-stage,
**planned — no code exists** idea: future games set in the Okaga fictional universe (chosen
because "the math of Obsmetrologia" fits it), built around a credits-as-warp economic conceit
(money = energy = time, so purchasing credits is what enables warp travel or other setting-native
"magic," skinning the shared Energy Bank ledger). **No specific new game is named for this vision
item** — it is not a request to rebuild this legacy Okaga game, and this note deliberately does
not merge the two. The legacy game above is a completed, playable-when-recovered artifact from a
specific setting; the vision item is an open invitation for *future, unwritten* games in that same
fictional universe. Placed on "The Stars (later)" shelf per `the-suite-and-the-studio.md` §3.

Task orchestrator's built-asset inventory §8, games/okaga; planned inventory item 20;
`gaming-enterprises-vision.md` §4; `the-suite-and-the-studio.md` §2–3.
